claims.text: Explicitly incorporating descriptors of local chemical and force-constant fluctuations will improve identification of low-lattice-thermal-conductivity high-entropy alloys relative to traditional models.
Local chemical fluctuations and force-constant variations are important mediators of phonon scattering in chemically disordered multi-element alloys.
The proposed approach applies to single-phase, chemically disordered solid-solution HEAs such as FeCoCrMnNi-type systems.
Relevant HEAs exhibit severe lattice distortion and force-constant fluctuations of approximately 20–50%.
The proposed approach transforms compositional inputs into expandable descriptors representing local chemical-fluctuation effects on phonon scattering.
Evaluation will cover room temperature and elevated temperatures while the alloys remain single-phase and chemically disordered.
Local chemical fluctuations produce force-constant distortions.
Force-constant fluctuations cause acoustic-phonon attenuation.
Enhanced phonon scattering suppresses lattice thermal conductivity.
Multi-element mixing induces severe lattice distortion that enhances phonon scattering.
Quantifying chemical-fluctuation descriptors will make predictions of phonon-transport suppression more accurate.
The approach will identify HEAs with lattice thermal conductivity near or below 1 W m−1 K−1.
The approach will improve predictive accuracy by at least 10–20% over conventional techniques lacking detailed disorder descriptors.
Current prediction methods are typically conventional ab initio or machine-learning models trained on simpler binary or ternary systems.
Current methods are less accurate for HEAs because of their complex chemical disorder.
The approach is applicable when an alloy is single-phase, chemically disordered, and has significant local force-constant fluctuations.
The approach may perform poorly for weakly disordered, multiphase, or strongly segregated alloys not represented by its descriptors.
The improvement magnitude and universality across HEA compositions remain uncertain pending systematic experimental validation.
The benchmark will compare predicted and measured lattice thermal conductivity, acoustic-phonon attenuation, dispersion, and GVDOS over multiple temperatures.
Failure to reduce prediction error by at least 10–20%, or consistent measured conductivities more than 20% above predictions, will falsify the hypothesis.
